### 01a0a1e7-2234-76a4-a596-cab3bb6fd2a4
- created: 2026-09-14T21:51:14Z | epoch: 1789422674.0
- status: completed | tags: docs,cli,worker:peerbox | parent: 
- summary:
CLI: restructure the gopi task command surface (solution B) — one home per function, no duplicate help for merger/worker, re-home git-infra and sync verbs

- spec/payload:
# CLI: restructure the `gopi task` command surface (complete solution B)

## Symptom (what the operator saw)

The operator read `gopi task -h` (captured at `/tmp/task_help.txt`, 418 lines /
26 KB) and reported it as "a kind of confusing", with a concrete example:

> the "task merger" sub command should belong to first order command "merger",
> right? why do we have separate help for same function? if I am reading
> `gopi merger --help`, do I read this task merge?

Both halves of that question are correct, and the source already confesses:

`cmd/agent/cli_tasks.go` tasksUsage, the `gopi task merger` block (task_help.txt
L366-370):

```
DEPRECATED ALIAS of the top-level 'gopi merger' (the merger is a
SERVICE, not a ledger verb — it was promoted out of this group for
exactly that reason). Still dispatched so running deployments and
scripts keep working; 'gopi task serve' is the older alias of the same
daemon. For the daemon's full contract see 'gopi merger -h'.
```

And `internal/taskverbs/verbs.go` header says the same thing in the design
layer:

```
SCOPE: the family verbs only. The group verb (`task`) and the top-level
resident services (worker, merger — peers of the group, documented in
their own index rows) are NOT family verbs and live in cmd/agent/cli_verbs.go.
```

So the *intent* (merger/worker are peers of the group, not family verbs) is
already written down — but the surface does not obey it:

- `taskverbs.Merger` is still a member of `FamilyVerbs` (verbs.go:122-127),
  i.e. advertised as a family verb.
- tasksUsage still documents `gopi task merger` across **three** Usage blocks
  (task_help.txt L350/351/355) plus a full daemon description.
- tasksUsage also documents **`gopi worker`** (L390) — the same error for the
  other resident service, which `taskverbs` explicitly names as a NON-family
  verb.
- `gopi merger -h` is a **separate, complete, cleaner** help (verified by
  running it: "GoPi merger — merge finished branches into master, then
  rebuild", with `--daemon`, `--once`, `--status`, `--stop`, `--restart`,
  `--start`, graceful-stop semantics, exit codes, privileges, sweep targets).

Result: **one function, two help texts, one of which declares itself
deprecated** — pure cognitive tax, zero information gain. Which one the
operator reads depends on which spelling they typed.

## Established by reading the surface (evidence, not guesswork)

The authoritative verb vocabulary is `internal/taskverbs/verbs.go` (Rule 14
leaf package — it exists exactly because the surface is documented in three
places that cannot import each other: `internal/config/help.go` top-level
index, `cmd/agent/cli_tasks.go` tasksUsage, and `cmd/agent/cli_completion.go`
`gopi task <TAB>` candidates). Two exported lists are load-bearing:

- `FamilyVerbs` — the ADVERTISED surface (help + completion), alphabetical.
  Currently 26 entries including `Merger`.
- `DispatchVerbs` — derived: `FamilyVerbs ∪ {Serve}`; every spelling the
  `runTasksSubcommand` switch must have a case for. Guarded by
  `TestTaskCompletionNamesMatchDispatch` (asserts exactly
  `FamilyVerbs ∪ {Serve}` equals the dispatcher's case labels) and
  `TestNoBareTaskVerbLiteralInDispatcher` (a bare literal in the dispatcher is
  treated as a DEFAULT, so the derivation cannot become a stale second
  definition).

Also established:

- `Merger`/`Worker` are already dispatched as **top-level** verbs
  (`cmd/agent/main.go:523` predicate chain: `isWorkerSubcommand`,
  `isMergerSubcommand`), and both have their own usage heads
  (`cmd/agent/main.go:216` `workerUsageHead`, `:388` `mergerUsageHead`).
- `Serve` is already the precedent for the correct treatment: it KEEPS a
  dispatch case for existing scripts, is **deliberately absent from
  `FamilyVerbs`**, and `TestTopLevelUsageTaskVerbEnumMatchesCompletion`
  asserts the top-level enumeration never carries it. That is exactly the
  shape the operator asked for — "still works, no longer taught".

### The actual structural problem: the group mixes five kinds of thing

Reading all 28 doc blocks in tasksUsage, the `gopi task` group is not one
group — it is five:

| Kind | Members | Should live |
|---|---|---|
| **true ledger verbs** (read/write a task row) | list, show, status, update, archive, tag-resumed, search, verdicts, submit, run, verify, reopen | `gopi task` ✔ |
| **resident services** | merger (deprecated alias), worker (duplicated) | their own top-level command only |
| **cross-node sync** | harvest, sync, diff, push | a sync surface of its own (it syncs the ledger, but it is a different product line) |
| **pure git infrastructure** (merger's internal atoms) | merge, merge-execute, adopt, audit-merges, merged-cleanup | documented under `gopi merger` (they ARE its pass) |
| **sweeps / maintenance** | sweep-zombies, sweep-worktrees, merged-cleanup, improvements | a maintenance surface |

The tell-tale: the help text of `adopt` / `merge` / `merge-execute` /
`audit-merges` / `merged-cleanup` each spends its prose describing the
**merger's** behaviour — e.g. "The serve daemon runs the same executor over
pending merge-backlog rows every pass, throttled to
`GOPI_MERGE_EXECUTE_INTERVAL`" and "the merger daemon's adoption pass always
submits" and "Direct infrastructure — no LLM child". Those are descriptions of
a *service's* pass, surfaced as if they were standalone operator verbs.

Second tell-tale: `gopi task list`'s block is 13 lines, of which **8 are about
`--sweep`** (the persisted 10-minute throttle stamp, the HP 2026-09-02
incident that motivated it, and when to run it with/without a daemon).
Implementation mechanism leaked into usage text. The user asked to list tasks.

## Deliverable

A **complete** restructure of the CLI's task-family surface so that:

1. **Each function has exactly ONE help text, at its canonical spelling.**
   `gopi merger -h` is the only merger help; `gopi worker -h` the only worker
   help. Reading `gopi task -h` must NOT teach merger/worker at all.
2. `gopi task` advertises only what it IS — the ledger verbs.
3. Every command that is currently dispatched **keeps working** (no behavior
   change, no breakage of deployments/scripts). Removing a spelling from
   *help* (and from the advertised completion surface) is the expected shape —
   see the `Serve` precedent and the `task new` precedent.
4. The restructure is enforced by the existing derivation tests rather than
   by discipline: after the change, a verb cannot be advertised in the wrong
   group without a test going red.

## Required work

### A. Establish the target surface first (write it down, get it reviewed)

Produce the target grouping as an explicit table in a devdoc:
`devdoc/cli-task-surface-restructure-20260915.md`. It must contain, for every
current spelling: `spelling → kind → canonical home → help owner → still
dispatched? (y/n)`. The five-kind table above is a *starting hypothesis* from
reading the help — correct it against the code (read the dispatch switch and
`cli_verbs.go`), and justify each move.

Design constraints to honour:

- **`FamilyVerbs` is presentation, `DispatchVerbs` is compatibility.** Move
  entries out of `FamilyVerbs` freely; a move is only safe if the spelling
  stays in `DispatchVerbs` (or keeps a dispatch case) so scripts keep working.
- **The single-source-of-truth discipline (Rule 13/14) must survive.** Do not
  hand-copy a verb list into a second place. If the new grouping needs new
  lists (e.g. a `MaintenanceVerbs`), they live in `internal/taskverbs` (or a
  sibling leaf package) and are DERIVED/asserted, never mirrored.
- **Top-level index consistency**: `internal/config/help.go`'s task row
  currently ENUMERATES `FamilyVerbs`. After the split, the index must describe
  the new groups correctly, and the equality tests
  (`TestTopLevelUsageTaskVerbEnumMatchesCompletion`,
  `TestTopLevelUsageShowsTaskLedger`, `TestFamilyVerbsMatchConstants`,
  `TestDispatchVerbsAreDerived`) must be updated to pin the NEW invariant —
  not deleted, and not weakened to "contains".

### B. Remove the duplicates

- `gopi task merger` and `gopi task worker` leave tasksUsage. Keep their
  dispatch cases so old spellings still run; the help should not mention them,
  in the same spirit as the `Serve` treatment. If a deprecation *hint* is kept
  anywhere, it belongs at the top-level command's help, not as a second usage
  block in the ledger group.
- Decide and document the fate of `gopi task serve` (the older alias, which
  today has a dispatch case but no Usage block at all).

### C. Re-home the misfiled entries

Per the target table: git infrastructure (merge / merge-execute / adopt /
audit-merges / merged-cleanup) should be documented where the merger's pass is
documented, and the sync family (harvest / sync / diff / push) should get its
own surface. The exact mechanism (new top-level group vs. a documented
subsection of an existing command vs. a move into `gopi merger -h`) is yours
to design — but the choice must be justified in the devdoc, and the resulting
help must be reachable by exactly one `-h` invocation.

### D. Trim the implementation leakage

`gopi task list`'s block must describe what the command does and its flags;
the `--sweep` throttle mechanism (persisted stamp window, incident history,
daemon interaction) belongs in the devdoc or the daemon's own help, not in the
user-facing usage of `list`. Same audit for every other block: keep the
contract, move the mechanism.

## Constraints

- **Work in a worktree from current master** (GOPI.md Rule 6a):
  `git worktree add ~/workspace/gopi-cli-surface -b feat/cli-task-surface-restructure`
- **Do NOT break the command surface.** Every spelling that runs today must
  still run. This is a help/grouping restructure, not a feature removal.
- **Do NOT weaken the derivation tests to make them pass.** If a test's
  invariant genuinely changes (because the surface genuinely changed), update
  it to pin the NEW invariant. Deleting a guard or relaxing it to "contains"
  is a failure, not a fix.
- **`gopi worker -h` / `gopi merger -h` must stay side-effect free** (the
  historic P0-1: `-h` must never start the loop; `isWorkerSubcommand` /
  `isMergerSubcommand` already guard this — do not regress it).
- Keep the GoPi single-binary / zero-new-dependency discipline. No new
  external tooling.
- Commit message in English; devdoc in the repo; commit as you go.

## What counts as done (machine-checkable)

1. `gopi task -h` contains **no** Usage block for `merger` or `worker`, and
   none for `serve`.
2. `gopi merger -h` and `gopi worker -h` remain the single, complete,
   reachable help for those two services (unchanged or improved, never
   reduced).
3. `go build ./...` and `go test ./cmd/agent/... ./internal/taskverbs/... ./internal/config/...`
   green — including the four derivation/index tests, updated to pin the new
   grouping.
4. A test exists that FAILS if someone re-adds a service (or a git-infra verb)
   to the ledger group's advertised surface. Name it in the devdoc. Show it
   red-then-green if practical.
5. Every currently-dispatched spelling still executes: list the checked ones
   in the devdoc with the actual command run (`gopi task merge --help` etc.),
   and confirm no spelling lost its dispatch case.
6. The devdoc contains the `spelling → kind → canonical home → dispatched?`
   table for the whole family (the "before/after" of the surface).
7. `gopi task list -h` (or `gopi task -h`'s list block) describes `list`'s
   behaviour and flags without the `--sweep` throttle mechanism.

## Why this is worth doing properly

The operator's reading cost is the product. The current surface makes him
re-read the same function twice, in two voices, and read internal mechanisms
(throttle stamps, daemon interaction) as if they were usage. The fix is not to
annotate the confusion — it is to make the surface have one home per function,
and to let the existing derivation tests hold that shape so it cannot drift
back.

If you find that the five-kind split is wrong (the code disagrees with the
reading), say so with file:line evidence and propose the corrected grouping —
the table is a hypothesis from reading help, not a mandate. An honest
correction beats a faithful implementation of a wrong grouping.

CLI-wide help dedup: apply the web_search deprecation contract (task serve pointer), resolve memsync vs memory sync, state the naming rule

- spec/payload:
# CLI-wide help deduplication: apply the `web_search` deprecation contract, resolve `memsync` vs `memory sync`

Companion to `brief-cli-task-surface-restructure.md` (task
`01a0a1e7-2234-76a4-a596-cab3bb6fd2a4`), which covers ONLY the `gopi task`
group. The operator asked whether the same "two help texts for one function"
disease exists elsewhere in gopi's help. **It does — three more cases.** This
brief covers them.

Full evidence, including what was checked and found clean:
`devdoc/cli-surface-audit-20260915.md` (commit `b93d17d3`). Read it first — it
has the `-h` transcripts and file:line anchors.

## The established contract (do not invent a new one)

`gopi web_search` / `gopi web_fetch` were already renamed to `gopi web search` /
`gopi web fetch` and handled **correctly**. Their treatment IS the CLI-wide
contract this task applies:

```
$ gopi web_search -h
note: gopi web_search is deprecated — use gopi web search

$ gopi web search -h
GoPi web search — expose the web_search tool as a CLI command.
```

Four properties, all of them load-bearing:

1. The old spelling **still dispatches** (script/deployment compatibility).
2. It prints **ONE pointer line** — never a second full help text.
3. The top-level `gopi -h` index advertises **only** the canonical spelling
   (`gopi -h` L97-98 show `web search`/`web fetch`, never the old spellings).
4. Both spellings are **pinned by the contract suite**:
   `cmd/agent/cli_contracts_test.go` `cliContractInventory` L77-78 tracks the
   deprecated spellings, L94-95 the canonical ones — so the compat surface is
   enforced by a test, not by memory.

## A. `gopi task serve` — give it the one-line pointer (mechanical)

**Now:** `gopi task serve -h` dumps the ENTIRE `gopi task` family usage.

**Should be:** one line like `web_search`'s — `note: gopi task serve is
deprecated — use gopi merger` (it is the older alias of the same daemon;
`internal/taskverbs/verbs.go` `Serve` comment says it is deliberately absent
from `FamilyVerbs`, and `TestTopLevelUsageTaskVerbEnumMatchesCompletion` asserts
the enumeration never carries it).

This is the same shape as Case A of the sibling brief. Keep the dispatch case.

## B. `gopi memsync` vs `gopi memory sync` — the real unfixed duplicate

**This is the only true duplicate-untouched pair on the whole CLI, and it is
worse than the merger case: neither help text mentions the other, and NEITHER
declares itself deprecated.** The operator sees both on adjacent lines of
`gopi -h` and cannot tell which to use:

```
  gopi memory <subcommand>    … and `gopi memory sync` for cross-node sync.
  gopi memsync                Node-to-node knowledge and ledger sync, as patch files.
```

Both move knowledge rows between nodes:

- `gopi memory sync --peer <alias>` — the newer **unique-only one-shot session**
  verb. Peers from `settings.json` `memory_peers` / `GOPI_MEMORY_PEERS`
  (deliberately decoupled from the ledger's `sync_peers`). Pushes our unique rows
  and pulls theirs in one invocation; rows present on both sides are NEVER
  touched (divergence is the declared out-of-scope conflict zone).
- `gopi memsync` — the older **patch-file** machinery. `--export`/`--import`
  (knowledge), `--export-proc`/`--import-proc` (procedural), plus **two things
  that are not sync at all**: `--export-tasks`/`--import-tasks` (the task-ledger
  patch channel) and `--dedup-scan` (an audit of twin rows — a maintenance verb
  wearing a sync command's name).

**Do NOT guess the resolution.** Investigate and then choose ONE, with evidence:

- **If `memsync` is superseded** → deprecate it exactly like `web_search`:
  keep every dispatch case, print ONE pointer line naming the replacement, drop
  it from the top-level index. Add a contract-suite entry for the deprecated
  spelling (mirroring L77-78).
- **If they do different jobs** (e.g. `memory sync` = live session verb;
  `memsync` = the patch-file/offline channel, still the only carrier for
  procedural and task patches) → then **each help must state the other's
  purpose in one line**, and `--dedup-scan` must move out of the sync surface
  (it is an audit; the sibling brief's "five kinds" analysis has a maintenance
  category for exactly this).

Evidence to gather for the decision: git history of both entry points
(when each was added, and by which design change), whether any live script /
hook / doc still calls the `memsync` spellings (grep the repo + `scripts/` +
`settings.json` consumers), and whether `memory sync` can express everything
`memsync --export-tasks` / `--export-proc` can. **If the evidence does not
settle it, report the finding with the evidence and your recommendation, and
leave the surface unchanged** — an honest "this needs an operator decision" is
a valid completion; inventing a deprecation the operator did not authorise is
not.

## C. Naming convention split (underscore vs dash/space)

The top-level index mixes styles with no stated rule, and the dash variants do
NOT work as aliases:

| underscore (tool-derived) | dash / space (hand-chosen) |
|---|---|
| `gopi vision_analyze` | `gopi code-search` |
| `gopi screen_capture` | `gopi scratch-gc` |
| `gopi voice_input` | `gopi web search` (space) |

The underscore spellings are exactly the ones lifted from `internal/toolnames`
(`ToolVisionAnalyze="vision_analyze"`, `ToolScreenCapture="screen_capture"`,
`ToolVoiceInput="voice_input"`), while `code-search`/`scratch-gc` are CLI verbs.
`text2img` is also a tool name but is one word, so it dodges the issue.

Two aggravating details:

- The help PROSE disagrees with the command SPELLING: `gopi voice_input -h`
  opens with "GoPi **voice input** — speech-to-text via Fun-ASR-Nano".
- The `web_search` → `web search` rename already chose the **space** form for a
  tool-named command, so the existing precedent points *away* from underscore —
  making `vision_analyze` / `screen_capture` / `voice_input` the outliers.

**Do:** state the rule explicitly in a devdoc, and either (a) normalise the three
underscore commands with the `web_search`-style deprecation treatment (old
spelling keeps dispatching, one-line pointer), or (b) document them as
deliberate exceptions **with the reason**. Either is acceptable; leaving the
inconsistency undocumented is not. Do NOT change a spelling without the
deprecation path — scripts exist.

## Constraints

- **Work in a worktree from current master** (GOPI.md Rule 6a):
  `git worktree add ~/workspace/gopi-cli-help-dedup -b feat/cli-help-dedup`
- **Coordinate with the sibling task** `01a0a1e7-2234-76a4-a596-cab3bb6fd2a4`
  (`brief-cli-task-surface-restructure.md`): it owns `cmd/agent/cli_tasks.go`
  tasksUsage and `internal/taskverbs`. **Case A above touches the SAME file**
  (`gopi task serve`'s help lives in tasksUsage). Check whether that task has
  landed; if its branch is in flight, keep your Case A change minimal and
  rebase, or fold Case A into its deliverable. Do not create two divergent
  rewrites of tasksUsage.
- **Never remove a dispatch case.** Every spelling that runs today must still
  run. This is help/grouping work, not feature removal.
- **Do not weaken the contract suite.** `cliContractInventory` entries are
  added for new/deprecated spellings, never deleted to silence drift
  (`TestCLIContractInventoryMatchesDispatch` is the guard).
- `-h` must stay side-effect free for every command you touch (the historic P0-1:
  a help flag must never start a loop or a daemon).

## What counts as done (machine-checkable)

1. `gopi task serve -h` prints a one-line pointer, not the family usage.
2. The `memsync` / `memory sync` question is **decided with evidence** and the
   surface reflects it — either a `web_search`-style deprecation (dispatch kept,
   one-line pointer, absent from the index, contract entry added) OR both helps
   cross-reference each other by purpose with `--dedup-scan` re-homed. If
   undecided, the devdoc reports the evidence and recommendation with the
   surface deliberately unchanged.
3. A written naming rule exists, and each of `vision_analyze` /
   `screen_capture` / `voice_input` either has the deprecation path or a
   documented exception reason.
4. `go build ./...` green; `go test ./cmd/agent/... ./internal/taskverbs/...
   ./internal/config/...` green (including the contract + index tests).
5. The devdoc lists, for every spelling touched: `old spelling → canonical →
   still dispatches? (y/n) → pinned by which test`.
6. Every spelling verified working by actually running it (show the commands and
   their first output line in the devdoc), including the deprecated ones.

## Why

The operator's reading cost is the product. One function must have one home and
one help text; a rename must leave a pointer, not a second manual. `web_search`
already demonstrates the contract — this task extends it to the places that
never got it, and pins it so the surface cannot drift back.

<!--row: 01a0a20b-c3f5-76b9-a712-3b77fabddada-->
### 01a0a20b-c3f5-76b9-a712-3b77fabddada
- created: 2026-09-14T22:31:15Z | epoch: 1789425075.0
- status: completed | tags: research,daemon,worker:peerbox | parent: 
- summary:
Research: the standard supported way to run a user daemon that survives logout on headless Linux (systemd user D-Bus absent) — cite upstream, verify on this host

- spec/payload:
# Research: the standard, supported way to run a long-lived user daemon that survives logout on a headless Linux host (no systemd user D-Bus)

> **WORKER-OWNERSHIP: OPERATOR-ONLY — devdoc/worker-ownership.md** — the operator owns this; an agent must never run it (submit the work instead: `gopi task submit`).

## Why this task exists

This problem has cost us repeated incidents over months and we have solved it four
times by hand, each time partially. The operator's framing is right: **this is a
traditional, decades-old problem — "run a daemon as a user that survives logout" —
and a standard answer must exist.** We want the standard answer, not another
bespoke workaround.

**This is a RESEARCH task.** Deliverable = the standard, documented solution,
evaluated against our host's measured constraints, with citations. Do NOT
implement a fix in this task (a follow-up implementation task will consume the
finding). The one exception: if you can *prove* with a command on this host that
one of the candidate mechanisms actually works end-to-end, that measurement is
the most valuable part of the deliverable — do it and record the transcript.

## The problem, stated precisely

We run long-lived background daemons as a normal user (uid 1000) on a headless
Linux box:

- `gopi merger --daemon` — a merge daemon that polls every 5 minutes
- `gopi worker --daemon` — a task worker

They are started from an **SSH session** (or from an agent's shell). They must
**keep running after that SSH session ends**, for days.

They do not. Measured, repeatedly:

```
# the daemon's own log, verbatim:
[merger] daemon: scope DEGRADED: still in a login session scope
         (/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-18200.scope)
         — this process dies with that scope
```

and later, its death:

```
[merger] force escalation: interrupting the in-flight pass now (reason: terminated received)
```

A daemon started 2026-09-14 07:02 was found dead ~23 hours later, having been
SIGTERM'd when its login session's scope was torn down. The operator was
surprised it was gone; the agent had wrongly assumed it was still polling.

### The root mechanism (already measured here — do not re-derive, verify if cheap)

`setsid` (which our detach path uses) makes the child a session leader with **no
controlling terminal**, but it **does not change the cgroup**. The daemon
therefore remains a member of `/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-N.scope`
(the login session's scope). When systemd tears that scope down — SSH closes,
the terminal goes away — **every process in the scope receives SIGTERM**,
daemon and children alike.

So `setsid` is a *real but partial* protection and the two properties must not be
conflated:

| property | does `setsid` give it? |
|---|---|
| no controlling terminal (no SIGHUP from the tty) | **yes** |
| survives the session scope's teardown | **no** ← this is the bug |

The correct, checkable verdict is always a fresh read of `/proc/<pid>/cgroup` —
never a mechanism's return value. (Our own code learned this the hard way: a
write to `cgroup.procs` returned success on this host while changing nothing.)

## The host's measured constraints (this is what makes the standard answer non-obvious)

Everything below was MEASURED on this host (Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15.0-163,
**cgroup v2 unified**, uid 1000), not read from documentation:

| candidate mechanism | result here |
|---|---|
| `systemd-run --user --scope …` (declarative, the textbook answer) | **FAILS**: `Failed to connect to bus: No such file or directory` |
| `ls /run/user/1000/bus` / `/run/user/1000/systemd/private` | **both ABSENT** — the user manager's private socket does not exist |
| `systemctl is-active user@1000.service` / `loginctl show-user nick` | **active** / **`Linger=yes`** — the manager RUNS and lingering is ON, but its **socket is absent** |
| re-probe from inside a real ssh session | **FAILS identically** — a new session does not create it either |
| `systemd-run --scope …` on the **system** bus | **FAILS** polkit: `Interactive authentication required` |
| `systemctl stop session-NNNNN.scope` (system or `--user`) | **FAILS** (polkit / no bus) — we cannot even tear down a session scope to test |
| `mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/<dir>` | **SUCCEEDS** — delegation is present (`cgroup.controllers` = `memory pids`) |
| `echo $$ > …/<dir>/cgroup.procs` | **EACCES**, although the dir is `nick nick 0664` |
| `/sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-1000.slice/` | `root:root 0755` — the kernel checks write permission on the **common ancestor**, which is why the self-migration write fails |

Current session, for reference: `cat /proc/self/cgroup` →
`0::/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-19205.scope`.

**The puzzle, precisely:** the *declarative* answer (`systemd-run --user`) needs a
D-Bus user manager socket that does not exist on this host; `Linger=yes` is on but
does not help because the socket is missing. So the standard answer appears
blocked — and yet this must be a solved problem.

Note the shape of the question this creates: **is the missing
`/run/user/1000/bus` the actual defect** (i.e. we should be fixing/finding *that*
— is it a broken PAM/mount, an ssh `UsePAM` issue, a `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` problem, a
`systemd --user` that never got started, logind's `KillUserProcesses`...)? If the
bus *should* be there, the correct solution may be to make it exist rather than
to work around its absence. **Investigate that line specifically** — it smells
like the real root cause.

## What we want from this research

1. **The standard, supported solution** for "user daemon surviving logout" on
   modern Linux with systemd, as documented by upstream (systemd docs, Arch Wiki,
   Debian/Ubuntu docs, `systemd.service(5)`, `loginctl(1)`, `systemd-run(1)`,
   `systemd-logind.conf(5)`) — with **URLs**. Cover the canonical mechanisms:
   `Linger` / `loginctl enable-linger`, `systemd --user` services, transient
   scopes (`systemd-run --user --scope`), `KillUserProcesses=no` in
   `logind.conf`, and what each one actually guarantees.
2. **Why the user bus is absent here** — is that expected or broken? What
   creates `/run/user/<uid>/bus`? Enumerate the known causes and give the
   diagnostic commands to identify ours. **If the fix is "the bus should exist",
   say exactly how to make it exist and how to verify.**
3. **What the recommended final architecture is** for this class of daemon
   (a systemd **user unit** with `WantedBy=default.target` + linger, vs
   `systemd-run --user --scope`, vs a system unit, vs something else) — and
   explicitly, **whether the operator should be doing this at all or whether it
   should be a system-level unit / cron / a supervisor**. Name the industry
   standard for "one person's headless box runs a polling daemon".
4. **The correct verification** — the command sequence that proves, on this host,
   that a daemon will survive logout. Ideally: start it, close the spawning
   session, confirm (a) the process lives, (b) `/proc/<pid>/cgroup` is NOT a
   `session-*.scope`, (c) it survives a second logout. Our acceptance for the
   follow-up task will be exactly this, so pin it down.
5. **The anti-patterns** — what people do that looks right and fails: `setsid`
   alone (ours), `nohup` alone, `disown`, `&` in a shell, `screen`/`tmux` hacks,
   writing to `cgroup.procs` (which *silently no-ops* on this host — we have the
   measurement), `daemon(3)`/double-fork alone. For each: what it does and does
   not protect.
6. **Privilege boundary** — which of the viable mechanisms need root and which do
   not, since our daemon must run as uid 1000 and our own help already promises
   "the merger needs NO privilege, `--daemon` included". If the standard answer
   needs root (or a sudoers/polkit rule), say so plainly — that is a finding, not
   a failure.

## What we already have (so you do not reinvent it, and can critique it)

We built a mechanism ladder, `cmd/agent/cli_daemon_scope.go`, with the escape
primitives in the zero-dependency leaf package `internal/cgroupscope/`:

1. `systemd-run --user --scope --unit=gopi-daemon-<face>` — when a user manager
   actually answers (probed with a real `systemd-run … /bin/true`, 5s budget)
2. in-process cgroupfs self-migration (`internal/cgroupscope`) — mkdir under the
   delegated subtree + write own pid + **verify by a fresh `/proc/self/cgroup` read**
3. `setsid` only, **DEGRADED**, with a loud warning — currently what actually happens here
4. `--require-scope` — hard refusal instead of a degraded start

Prior write-up: `devdoc/daemon-cgroup-detach-20260913.md` (the measurements table
above is drawn from it); also `devdoc/no-privilege-daemon.md`,
`devdoc/daemon-scope-privilege-hint-20260914.md`.

**Critique this ladder against the standard answer.** If the standard solution is
"enable linger and install a user unit", then our ladder's rung 3 is not a
solution at all and rungs 1–2 are workarounds for a host misconfiguration —
**say that plainly if it is true.** An honest "your ladder is treating the
symptom; here is the actual cause and the documented fix" is the best possible
outcome of this task.

## Constraints

- **Research task: do not implement.** Report the finding with citations + the
  host-specific verdict. The follow-up implementation is a separate task.
- **Verify against THIS host where cheap.** A documented mechanism that you also
  ran here (with the transcript) beats a citation alone. Do not merely assert.
- **Respect the sandbox:** do not start long-lived daemons that outlive the
  session, do not change system configuration (`logind.conf`, linger state, PAM),
  do not use `sudo` unless the task truly requires it — if a proposed fix needs
  root, describe it and mark it as requiring the operator. Read-only probing is
  expected and encouraged.
- **Work in a worktree from master** (GOPI.md Rule 6a):
  `git worktree add ~/workspace/gopi-daemon-research -b research/daemon-survives-logout`
- Cite **upstream/authoritative** sources (systemd man pages / freedesktop docs /
  Arch or Debian wiki), not LLM-generated blogspam. If a source is a blog, say
  why it is trustworthy, or mark it as secondary.
- If you use `web_search`/`web_fetch`, note that the operator's guidance is that
  certain sites may be unreachable; prefer authoritative docs mirrors and record
  what you could not reach.

## What counts as done

1. A devdoc (`devdoc/daemon-survives-logout-research.md`) containing:
   - **The recommended solution**, stated in one paragraph up front, with URLs.
   - The **root cause of the absent user bus** on this host, with the diagnostic
     evidence and the exact fix (or an explicit "cause could be one of N — here
     is the command that distinguishes them").
   - A **comparison table**: mechanism → what it guarantees → needs root? →
     works on THIS host (measured Y/N/?).
   - The **verification recipe** (command sequence proving survival of logout).
   - The **anti-pattern list** with what each one fails to protect.
2. At least **6 authoritative citations** with URLs.
3. Where you probed this host, the **verbatim command + observed output**.
4. An explicit **critique of our existing ladder** — does it match the standard
   answer, is it a workaround for a misconfiguration, should anything be deleted?
5. A short **"what the follow-up implementation task should do"** section (a
   checklist), since a separate task will consume this.
6. **Not Done / honest limits** — anything you could not determine, especially if
   the absence of the bus could not be conclusively explained without root.

## Context the operator cares about

His words: *"it has puzzled us for so long and it is such a traditional issue
that I am pretty sure it has solution as it is not a new one."* He wants the
**standard** answer — the thing a competent sysadmin would do — not a fifth
bespoke workaround. Optimise for: does a documented, supported path exist, and
what is it.

gopi merger should always rebuild binary whenever new branch is merged. this is by default, but I suspect this is only done at worktree before merging successful. meaning my observation is that everytime I build gopi, it can take some time to finish, this proves it is not rebuilt. checking binary gopi binary time can prove this. make sure this rebuilding is done after merger receives child gopi process success/failure return.



<!--row: 01a0a4a9-28bd-7037-8ea3-e7828fce3589-->
### 01a0a4a9-28bd-7037-8ea3-e7828fce3589
- created: 2026-09-15T10:42:24Z | epoch: 1789468944.0
- status: completed | tags: bug,storage,worker:peerbox | parent: 
- summary:
merger build gate: move GOCACHE/GOMODCACHE out of the tmpfs scratch onto disk (reusable cache, not disposable storage) — /dev/shm hit 100% at 1.1G per build

- spec/payload:
# Merger build gate: stop writing GOCACHE/GOMODCACHE into the tmpfs scratch — move both to disk

> **WORKER-OWNERSHIP: OPERATOR-ONLY — devdoc/worker-ownership.md** — the operator owns this; an agent must never run it (submit the work instead: `gopi task submit`).

## Symptom (measured today, 2026-09-15)

`/dev/shm` (tmpfs, **7.8G = half of RAM, pages not write-backable**) filled to **100%**
with 2.1M free. This is an OOM hazard, not a cosmetic problem: exceeding tmpfs does not
swap, it invokes the host OOM killer.

Cleaned to 15% by hand. The residue's shape:

```
$ du -sh /dev/shm/*        # before cleanup
6.3G    /dev/shm/gopi-test-scratch
...
$ du -sh /dev/shm/gopi-test-scratch/*
4.5G    queue
$ du -sh /dev/shm/gopi-test-scratch/queue/queue-runtime-merge-build-2712346/*
726M    .../gocache
410M    .../gomodcache                      <- 1.2G for ONE merger run
```

415 directories under `queue/`, one per dead merger pid; each carries a `gocache` +
`gomodcache` pair. **The merger's build gate writes its Go caches into the tmpfs scratch**,
so every merger build costs ~1.1G of RAM-backed storage, and every crashed merger leaves
its own copy behind.

**Why the existing GC does not save us** (also measured): the sweep runs correctly every 30
minutes and reports `removed=0`, eight consecutive ticks:

```
18:00:01 scratch-gc-watchdog ... removed=0 stale=6h0m0s disabled=false
18:30:01 scratch-gc-watchdog ... removed=0 stale=6h0m0s disabled=false
```

`internal/scratch/gc.go:55-60` sets `StaleAge = 6 * time.Hour`, with the comment
*"longer than any healthy suite run (the whole GoPi test tree is minutes)"*. That assumption
is stale: `cmd/agent` now carries 20m/25m/40m timeouts, `internal/tools` runs 100-500s, and
suites + merger + worker create scratch concurrently. **A 6h window cannot bound a tree whose
producer rate is ~1.1G per merger build.** (That is a separate concern — a `StaleAge` knob —
and is NOT the main ask here; see "Not in scope".)

## The ask: the caches do not belong in a tmpfs scratch at all

**Operator's framing (2026-09-15):** *"构建缓存是跨任务复用的资产，scratch 是用完即弃的"* —
a build cache is a **cross-task reused asset**; scratch is **use-and-discard**. Putting the
former inside the latter is wrong on both counts:

- **Wastefully**: a discarded cache forces a cold recompile. Measured in-tree:
  `merge_build_gate.go:407` — *"68s for a stdlib+sqlite build from a cold GOCACHE against ~2s
  warm"*. So the current placement pays up to 68s per build **and** throws the result away.
- **Dangerously**: 1.1G per build into a 7.8G RAM-backed filesystem, unswappable. Two
  concurrent merger builds plus a test suite is a meaningful fraction of the whole budget.

**Target:** both caches live on disk, under the repo/workspace area (the `~/workspace/` family
that exists precisely so heavy artifacts never land on `/` or in tmpfs — see GOPI.md /
`devdoc/pa-shell-discipline-*` precedent), **not** in `internal/scratch`'s tmpfs root.

## What exists today (read this before designing — the author already reasoned about it)

`internal/tools/merge_build_gate.go:402-430` `mergeBuildGateGoCache()`, verbatim intent:

> It is deliberately per-PROCESS, not per-call: a per-call cache would make every branch pay a
> cold toolchain compile (MEASURED on this host: 68s … against ~2s warm) while the gate runs
> once per branch per tick. **It lives in the runtime scratch class, never in the operator's
> ~/.cache — a merge probe must not fill the user's build cache**, and it must not depend on it
> either.

and `internal/tools/merge_build_gate_modcache.go` (commit `455daa77`, already on master):

> **THE FIX: the build RESOLVES ITS MODULES BY CONSTRUCTION** — GOMODCACHE is pointed at a
> populated, READ-ONLY, operator-owned module cache, so there is no fetch to attempt in the
> first place. … GOCACHE stays inside the gate's own per-process scratch … so a merge probe
> still cannot fill the user's BUILD cache, and the shared module cache is used read-only.

So the current design has **two documented goals that are in tension with today's symptom**:

| goal | why |
|---|---|
| do NOT fill the operator's cache (`~/.cache/go-build`, 88G; `~/go/pkg/mod`, 1.9G) | a merge probe writing into the caches the operator's own builds read is a real hazard |
| keep the cache per-process & disposable | isolation between concurrently-gated branches |

and it **solved the module half already**: `mergeBuildGateSharedModCache()` returns the
operator's `go env GOMODCACHE` **read-only**, and the scratch `gomodcache` is now only a
fallback for a repo that is *not* a Go module (`merge_build_gate.go:306-318`). Measured on
master today:

```
$ go env GOMODCACHE GOCACHE
/home/user/go/pkg/mod
/home/user/.cache/go-build
```

**So the 410M scratch `gomodcache` in today's residue is largely historical** (from before
`455daa77`, or from the non-Go-repo fallback path) — confirm which before treating it as a
live cost. **The 726M `gocache` is the live one.**

## The design question to settle

The gate needs a **warm, shared, per-repo Go BUIILD cache that lives on disk** and that a merge
probe may write without corrupting or bloating the operator's own cache. Design it, and justify
the choice against the two existing goals above. Candidate shapes (not a mandate — argue):

1. **A dedicated disk location owned by the gate**, e.g. `<repo>/.gocache-mergegate` (inside the
   repo, gitignored) or `~/workspace/gopi-mergegate-cache/<repo>` — shared across builds and
   PIDs, on disk, never tmpfs, never the operator's cache.
2. **The operator's cache but scoped**, e.g. `GOCACHE=<operator cache>/mergegate` — keeps warm
   reuse from the shared module/root while isolating writes to a subdirectory.
3. **Something else** — if you find a documented Go-idiomatic answer (the toolchain has
   `GOCACHE` semantics worth reading: it is content-addressed and safe for concurrent use; the
   real hazard is *using* the operator's cache as a write target vs. inheriting its warmth).

**Hard constraints on the answer:**

- **Never tmpfs, never `/`.** The scratch root ban (Rule 22 / the 2026-09-11 exhaustion) is
  exactly what today's incident re-proved. A disk path under `$HOME` is required.
- **Bounded growth.** A shared cache grows forever. State the bound (size cap, or reuse an
  existing sweep) and how it is enforced. An unbounded 726M-per-build cache on disk is a
  different incident waiting to happen.
- **Concurrency-safe.** The gate runs per branch per tick and the merger is not the only
  writer on this host. Go's build cache is designed for concurrent use — say so if you rely on
  it, and cite the reason.
- **No new dependency, no privilege** (the merger's contract is `--daemon` with no privilege).
- **Do not regress the module resolution** already fixed by `455daa77` (read-only shared
  GOMODCACHE), and do not break the non-Go-repo fallback path.

## Also required

- **Verify the reuse claim, do not assume it.** The whole point is warmth. Measure: run a gate
  build twice against the new location and show the second is warm (the in-tree reference is
  "68s cold vs ~2s warm" — reproduce or refute). Report the numbers.
- **A regression proof for the hazard.** Show that a gate build no longer creates anything
  under the tmpfs scratch root: e.g. assert no `gocache`/`gomodcache` appears under
  `scratch.RuntimeScratchDir(...)` during a gate run. If a test can express "the gate's build
  cache is not in the scratch tree", write it.
- **Report the tmpfs budget explicitly** in the devdoc: what a single gate build used to cost
  in `/dev/shm` (measured today: 1.14G) and what it costs after.
- If you conclude the **existing placement is actually correct** and today's full tmpfs was
  caused by something else (e.g. only the GC's 6h window, or a leaked test scratch), **say so
  with measurements** and propose the alternative fix. The operator's premise is that a
  reusable cache does not belong in use-and-discard storage — that is sound reasoning, but the
  fix must be aimed at the measured cause, not at the reasoning.

## Constraints

- Work in a worktree from current master (GOPI.md Rule 6a):
  `git worktree add ~/workspace/gopi-mergegate-cache -b fix/mergegate-cache-on-disk`
- **Do not touch `/dev/shm` content by hand** — the operator cleaned it; a task must not delete
  tmpfs entries as part of this work. Read it for measurement only.
- `internal/tools` is large and slow; use `-run` filters for iteration and a bounded timeout
  for the full package (a plain `go test ./internal/tools/` needs ~100-500s and, under load,
  can trip a goroutine-dump FAIL that is a host-load artifact — treat an isolated re-run as the
  verdict, and say so if you hit it).
- Commit as you go; devdoc in the repo.

## Not in scope (do not fix these here — they are separate tasks)

- `internal/scratch/gc.go` `StaleAge = 6h` being too long, and it being a hardcoded constant
  with no knob. Real, worth its own task; **mention it in the devdoc as a related finding** but
  do not change it here (a GC change and a cache-relocation change in one diff cannot be
  attributed when something goes wrong).
- The 415-directory residue count / a one-off cleanup script.

## Done means

1. The gate's Go **build** cache (and, if still used, its module cache) is a **disk** path —
   demonstrated by command + path, not asserted. Nothing cache-shaped is created under the
   tmpfs scratch root by a gate run.
2. Growth is **bounded**, and the bound is stated with how it is enforced.
3. The **warmth** claim is measured (second build fast), with numbers.
4. A test (or a documented, reproducible command) fails/asserts the old behaviour — i.e. the
   regression is pinned, not just fixed.
5. A devdoc records: the measured before/after tmpfs cost, the chosen location and WHY
   (against the two pre-existing goals quoted above), the bound, and the related-but-deferred
   `StaleAge` finding.
6. `go build ./...` green, affected packages' tests green, and the **non-Go-repo fallback** and
   **read-only shared GOMODCACHE** behaviours explicitly re-verified as unchanged.
7. Anything you could not determine, declared in a Not Done section.

## Why this matters beyond one incident

This is the third time storage placement has caused an outage on this host (`/` in 2026-08 and
2026-09, tmpfs today). The pattern is always the same: a **growing artifact** placed in storage
sized for **transient** data. The merge gate's cache is a clean instance — reusable by nature,
discarded by placement. Getting it onto disk with a bound is the generalisable fix, and it
removes 1.1G per merger build from the most fragile filesystem we have.



<!--row: 01a0a4b8-5b4d-7d8a-a818-0471e9bcb37f-->
### 01a0a4b8-5b4d-7d8a-a818-0471e9bcb37f
- created: 2026-09-15T10:59:00Z | epoch: 1789469940.0
- status: failed | tags: bug,daemon,worker:peerbox | parent: 
- summary:
Find the actor that unlinked /run/user/1000/{bus,systemd/private} (user bus broken → daemons died with their login scope) + guard against recurrence

- spec/payload:
# Find the unlink of /run/user/1000/{bus,systemd/private} — the actor that breaks the user bus, and stop it recurring

> **WORKER-OWNERSHIP: OPERATOR-ONLY — devdoc/worker-ownership.md** — the operator owns this; an agent must never run it (submit the work instead: `gopi task submit`).

## Why this task exists

On 2026-09-15 the **user bus on this host was found with its socket files unlinked while the
kernel still had them bound**. Consequence: `systemd-run --user --scope` failed, so gopi's
daemons could not leave the login-session cgroup, so `gopi merger --daemon` / `gopi worker
--daemon` kept dying whenever their SSH session's scope was torn down — a months-old,
repeatedly-misdiagnosed problem.

**The bus has been repaired by hand** (see "Already done" below) and the mechanism is now
understood. **This task is about the ACTOR**: what unlinked those paths, and how do we stop it
recurring. The research report explicitly left this open — it is not a gap in that work, it is
the next question.

## The measured state (do not re-derive; verify cheaply if useful)

From `devdoc/daemon-survives-logout-research.md` (41KB, task `01a0a20b`) and its probe set
`devdoc/daemon-survives-logout-probes/` (p1–p14) + `devdoc/userbus-diagnosis-probes/`:

The sockets were **bound in the kernel, unlinked from the filesystem**:

```
# /proc/net/unix  (kernel state — readable without privilege)
0000000000000000: 00000002 00000000 00010000 0001 01 39144 /run/user/1000/systemd/private
0000000000000000: 00000000 00000000 00010000 0001 01 40136 /run/user/1000/bus   # + 8 connected

# but on the filesystem:
stat: cannot statx '/run/user/1000/bus': No such file or directory
connect() -> ENOENT
```

with the holders **still alive**: the user manager (pid 2321) fd 19 → `socket:[39144]`, fd 27 →
`socket:[40136]`; `dbus-daemon` (pid 2342) fd 3 → `socket:[40136]`; and no process on the host
whose filesystem view carries the path (`visible_in_any_process=0`).

**Ruled out by measurement** (so do not re-investigate these):

- `logind.conf` / linger / PAM misconfiguration — all stock, `Linger=yes`, no (`no` for the
  control user).
- A separate mount namespace — the manager, dbus-daemon and the shell all share `mnt:[4026531841]`.
- A permission artifact — a `sudo`-level listing of the manager's own view shows only
  `inaccessible/`.
- A host-wide policy — **uid 117 (lightdm) still has `/run/user/117/{bus,systemd/private,systemd/notify}` bound**,
  so the loss is **uid-1000-specific**.

Two mtime brackets exist but neither names an actor, and the journal windows are empty:

```
/run/user/1000          2026-09-14 22:39:10
/run/user/1000/systemd  2026-09-15 07:26:18
```

## The two candidate mechanisms the report could not separate (start here)

1. **`internal/testutil.legacy_residue.go`** — a sweep that collects legacy suite-scratch roots
   by the rule *"`gopi-` prefix AND `suite-tmp-` infix"* under a base directory, calling
   `os.RemoveAll` (`legacy_residue.go:184`). The base is `MemoryBase()` =
   `GOPI_SCRATCH_MEMORY_BASE` else `worktreeroots.ShmDir` (= `/dev/shm`). **Note the guards it
   already has** (`SuiteTempRootOverride()` non-empty ⇒ sweep nothing; the namespace rule keeps
   it bounded to `gopi-*suite-tmp-*`) — so if this is the actor, the question is **how the base
   or a caller's root came to be the runtime dir**, not that the rule is unbounded.
2. **`GOPI_TEST_TMPDIR` / `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` being pointed at the runtime dir by a run** — the
   report names the same-host `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/tmp/tabpoc/rt` pattern as the shape that would
   match, i.e. a run whose scratch *root* was the runtime directory, so its cleanup
   (`os.RemoveAll(root)`) removed the sockets.

**Also worth checking (do not assume):** anything else on this host that writes into
`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` and then sweeps it — `systemd-tmpfiles` rules, cron/timers, the
`scratch-gc` watchdog (`~/.local/bin/gopi-scratch-gc-watchdog.sh`, a cron job every 30 min),
`internal/scratch/gc.go`'s sweep, or a gopi test that pins a scratch root at the runtime dir.
The report ruled out "gopi's default root lists" — extend that by enumerating **every**
`os.RemoveAll` reachable from a path that could be `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or its parent.

## What we want

1. **Name the actor, or prove it is unnameable.** If you can reproduce it, do — a reproduction
   is the strongest possible evidence. If it cannot be reproduced, say so and give the
   reasoning that narrows it to a class, with the commands that distinguish the remaining
   candidates. **"Could not determine, here is why and here is what would settle it" is an
   acceptable outcome**; a confident guess is not.
2. **A guard that makes the recurrence impossible or loud**, in whichever layer the actor turns
   out to live. The property to protect, stated as an invariant:

   > No code path in this repo may `os.RemoveAll` (or otherwise unlink) a path that is, or is
   > under, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, nor a path whose children include a live socket the user manager
   > is bound to.

   Prefer a **test** that fails if a sweep's root can ever be the runtime dir over a comment. If
   you find such a path exists today, that IS the finding — show the call chain.
3. **A cheap detector for the failure mode**, so this never again presents as "mystery daemon
   death". The diagnosis was hard because the evidence is kernel-side while the symptom is
   filesystem-side. Something like a check that `stat`s `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/{bus,systemd/private}`
   and, if absent, greps `/proc/net/unix` for the bound inode and says
   **"bound but path unlinked — the manager is alive; the runtime dir was emptied; restart
   user-runtime-dir@<uid>.service"**. gopi already has a probe that emits roughly this
   (`cmd/agent/daemon_userbus_probe.go`); the ask is to make it reachable when the operator needs
   it (e.g. from the daemon start path's refusal message, or a documented verb) rather than only
   from a research transcript. Judge whether that is worth adding, and say so honestly if it is
   not.

## Already done (context — do not redo)

The bus was repaired by the operator/agent on 2026-09-15, and **verified working**:

```
sudo systemctl restart user-runtime-dir@1000.service    # recreated the runtime dir + socket files
sudo systemctl stop    user@1000.service                # the old instance was degraded
sudo systemctl start   user@1000.service                # first attempt failed 219/CGROUP (left-over pulseaudio
                                                        #   in the cgroup); succeeded once the orphan exited
systemctl is-active user@1000.service                   # -> active

systemd-run --user --scope --quiet --unit=probe /bin/true      # -> exit 0
cat /proc/self/cgroup   # -> 0::/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/probe-….scope
                        #    NOT session-N.scope  == the escape finally works
```

**Second finding, keep it:** the first `start` failed with `status=219/CGROUP` because of a
**left-over process in the unit's control group**:

```
user@1000.service: Found left-over process 309635 (pulseaudio) in control group while starting
unit. Ignoring.
user@1000.service: This usually indicates unclean termination of a previous run.
user@1000.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=219/CGROUP
```

So "restart user@1000.service" can legitimately need **one retry** — report that as an operator
note if your investigation confirms it, since a single-shot restart looks like a failure.

## Constraints

- Work in a worktree from current master (GOPI.md Rule 6a):
  `git worktree add ~/workspace/gopi-userbus-actor -b fix/userbus-unlink-actor`
- **Read-only on the host's live state.** Do NOT unlink/restart anything belonging to the
  session's own bus, do NOT stop or restart `user@1000.service` or `user-runtime-dir@1000.service`
  (you would kill the desktop session and the operator's shells), and do NOT modify
  `logind.conf`, PAM, tmpfiles rules or cron. If a proposed fix needs root, describe it and mark
  it operator-gated.
- A reproduction, if you build one, must run in its **own** isolated runtime dir (e.g.
  `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=` a temp dir) — never against `/run/user/1000`.
- Devdoc in the repo; commit as you go.

## Not in scope

- Re-landing the fix (nothing is broken now).
- Re-litigating the research report's conclusions — treat them as measured input.
- The `internal/scratch` `StaleAge = 6h` constant (separate concern, already noted elsewhere).

## Done means

1. A devdoc `devdoc/userbus-unlink-actor.md` stating: the actor (named, or the narrowed class
   with the commands that distinguish the rest), the evidence, and the honest limits.
2. Either **a test/guard that pins the invariant above** (preferred), or a documented reason why
   a guard is not the right layer — with the alternative check if so.
3. A reproduction **or** an explicit statement that none could be produced plus what would settle
   it (e.g. an auditd watch on the path, if the operator is willing).
4. The operator-restart note (the 219/CGROUP retry) recorded in the devdoc if your work confirms it.
5. `go build ./...` green; tests for any package you touch green; a Not Done section.

### 01a0a4c4-c26a-726f-a32f-72b171194741
- created: 2026-09-15T11:12:33Z | epoch: 1789470753.0
- status: failed | tags: bug,storage,worker:peerbox | parent: 
- summary:
scratch GC: the stale window is a hardcoded 6h constant whose stated assumption is false — parameterise it or size a budget instead of a time window

- spec/payload:
# scratch GC: the stale window is a hardcoded 6h constant whose stated assumption is false — parameterise it and stop sizing a time window instead of a budget

> **WORKER-OWNERSHIP: OPERATOR-ONLY — devdoc/worker-ownership.md** — the operator owns this; an agent must never run it (submit the work instead: `gopi task submit`).

## Why this task exists, and what it is NOT

On 2026-09-15 `/dev/shm` (7.8G tmpfs, unswappable) reached **100% full** and started failing
builds/tests with `database or disk is full (13)` / `no space left on device`. An operator cleaned
it by hand (100% → 15%, 6.6G).

**Four sibling tasks already own four distinct defects of that incident. This task is the fifth
gap, and it is the only one nobody has claimed.** Read the list before you start so you do not
duplicate or contradict them:

| task | owns |
|---|---|
| `01a0a411` | agent-created ad-hoc dirs written **directly** into /dev/shm, outside the scratch home (702 entries / 2.6G) — no sweeper ever plans them |
| `01a0a40b-5c5b` | **marker-less queue children** inside the scratch home (415MB + ~454MB) — `IsScratchEntry` requires a marker, so they are invisible to the sweep |
| `01a0a429` | verification **worktrees** under the memory base are outside every declared policy root |
| `01a0a42d` | `settings.json` `tmpdir` is **UNSET** so children inherit `os.TempDir()` → `/tmp` on the `/` partition (4.0G never-reaped) |
| `01a0a4a9` | merger build gate writes GOCACHE/GOMODCACHE into the tmpfs scratch (1.1G per build) |

**The gap all five share, and which none of them fixes:** the GC's **stale window**.
`internal/scratch/gc.go:55-60`:

```go
// StaleAge is the age past which an unheld scratch directory is garbage.
// Six hours: longer than any healthy suite run (the whole GoPi test tree is
// minutes), short enough that a morning's leftovers are gone by the
// afternoon.
StaleAge = 6 * time.Hour
```

Two problems, both measured today:

1. **The stated premise is false.** *"the whole GoPi test tree is minutes"* — `cmd/agent` now
   carries 20m/25m/40m timeouts, `internal/tools` runs 100–500s, and suites + merger + worker
   create scratch **concurrently**. A 6h window cannot bound a tree whose producer rate is
   1.1G per merger build plus multiple parallel suites.
2. **It is a hardcoded constant with exactly one writer and no reader.** `grep StaleAge` finds
   only its own definition and a sibling in the same file (verified on master today). Compare
   `GCIntervalEnvName = "GOPI_TEST_SCRATCH_GC_MIN"`, which IS a documented knob for the sweep's
   *cadence* — so the system already accepts that this has an operator-tunable dimension, and
   the *threshold* was simply never given one. **That asymmetry is the defect.**

**The evidence that this is live, not theoretical** — the sweep runs correctly and reports
nothing to do, eight consecutive ticks, while the filesystem fills:

```
18:00:01 scratch-gc-watchdog scratch-gc role=cli home=/dev/shm/gopi-test-scratch removed=0 stale=6h0m0s disabled=false
18:30:01 scratch-gc-watchdog scratch-gc role=cli home=/dev/shm/gopi-test-scratch removed=0 stale=6h0m0s disabled=false
```

(`~/.gopi/logs/scratch-gc-watchdog.log`; the watchdog is the cron job installed by
`scripts/install-scratch-gc-watchdog.sh`, every 30 min, which invokes `gopi scratch-gc`.)
A mechanism that is healthy and a policy that is wrong look identical from the outside — this
task is about the policy.

## The design question

**Do not simply change 6h to 1h.** That is the same mistake with a different number, and Rule 1
forbids unexplained magic values. The question is: what SHOULD decide that a scratch entry is
reclaimable?

Candidate axes — argue for one, with measurements, rather than listing them back:

1. **Operator-tunable threshold** (the `GCIntervalEnvName` precedent): env + `settings.json`,
   three-layer `CLI > env > settings` like the other knobs, with the 6h as the documented
   default. Cheapest, consistent with the codebase, but still time-based.
2. **Capacity/pressure-driven** (the axis that actually matches the failure): the filesystem
   filled in **6 hours**, so *time* is the wrong unit for a resource measured in **bytes**.
   Something like "reclaim unheld entries oldest-first while the scratch tree exceeds a
   high-water mark", or a shorter window that tightens as the tree grows. Fixes the class, not
   the instance.
3. **Held-ness instead of age.** An entry an in-flight suite holds is already recognised (the
   `IsScratchEntry`/holder machinery, and `SweepHome`'s ownership arm). If liveness is knowable,
   an unheld entry is arguably garbage *immediately* — age is a proxy for "is anyone using it",
   and the code may already have the real answer. **Check this first**; if true it makes both
   time and capacity moot and is by far the best finding available in this task.

**Whatever you choose, the hard constraints:**

- **Never a global delete.** The namespace limit (`IsScratchEntry` markers, `SweepHome` walking
  only the resolved scratch home) is load-bearing — `01a0a411`/`01a0a40b` exist precisely
  because things outside it are NOT collectable, and the fix for those must come from their
  owners, not from widening this sweep. Do not free foreign trees to make /dev/shm emptier.
- **Never `/`, never `/tmp`, never the run-time directory.** Rule 22. A too-aggressive sweep is
  strictly worse than a too-lax one: `01a0a4b8` is chasing an unlink of
  `/run/user/1000/{bus,systemd/private}` that killed the user bus for a day — the leading
  hypothesis is a sweep whose root reached outside its own tree. **Do not become that actor.**
- **The bound must be argued, not chosen.** State what a safe window is, from measured producer
  rates and suite durations on this host, and what it costs (a too-short window reaps a suite's
  live scratch → exactly the class of bug this codebase has been fighting).
- **Keep the existing semantics:** unheld + older-than-window = garbage; a **held** entry is
  never reclaimed regardless of age (`SweepHome`'s ownership arm, `gc.go:101`'s EACCES
  handling, the `GCUnreadableScratchEntryDoesNotPanic` case). A change that reaps a held entry
  is a regression, not a fix.

## Also required

- **A test that would have caught today.** Assert the property, not the number: e.g. "given a
  producer rate of R and a filesystem of size S, an unheld entry older than the window is
  reclaimed before the tree can reach S" is too abstract to test — so instead pin the
  *mechanism*: (a) an entry older than the configured window is collected, (b) an entry younger
  than it is kept, (c) a **held** entry is kept regardless of age, (d) whatever knob you add
  actually changes the behaviour end-to-end (a test that sets it to a tiny value and observes
  collection). (d) is the one that matters — a knob with no reader is the defect you are fixing.
- **Report, in the devdoc, the measured numbers** that justify the value: `du` of the scratch
  tree over a period, the suite durations on this host, and the size at which the tree reached
  100%. If you adopt a pressure-driven design, show the hysteresis/watermark reasoning.
- **Do not clean up the current live residue as part of this task.** The operator handled it;
  deleting tmpfs content here destroys the evidence the sibling tasks are using.

## Constraints

- Work in a worktree from current master (GOPI.md Rule 6a):
  `git worktree add ~/workspace/gopi-scratch-staleage -b fix/scratch-gc-stale-window`
- `internal/scratch` is a leaf package with a focused test suite — keep it that way. If your
  knob needs plumbing through `internal/config` + `cmd/agent`, follow the existing
  `GCIntervalEnvName` pattern exactly (Rule 2: one reader per name; Rule 13/14: constants in
  the leaf package).
- If the honest answer is **"the window is not the real problem — the four sibling tasks are, and
  once they land the 6h window is fine"**, say exactly that with measurements and propose only
  the minimal change (at most exposing the knob). An argument against doing work is a valid
  deliverable; a speculative redesign is not.

## Done means

1. A devdoc `devdoc/scratch-gc-stale-window.md` with: the chosen design, the argument for it
   (against the three axes above), and the **measured numbers** it rests on.
2. The window/threshold is **no longer a bare constant with no reader** — either it is
   configurable and something reads it, or the replacement mechanism is demonstrably live.
3. Tests covering collect / keep-young / keep-held / the-knob-actually-works, with the
   knob-effect test red before the change if you add a knob.
4. No regression in the held-entry guarantee (`SweepHome` ownership arm, EACCES/unreadable
   handling).
5. `go build ./...` green; `internal/scratch` and any package you touch green; the standard
   gates green (`go vet ./...` at minimum — note this repo has had a master red that
   `go build` could not see because test files are not part of the build).
6. A Not Done section, and an explicit statement of how this task's change relates to the four
   sibling tasks (does it make any of them unnecessary? does it depend on one?).
